head.eyebrow: 03 · How a support claim is built
head.title: GitHub issues six kinds of token. Which ones do you catch?
head.lede: Answering that honestly is the entire job of this structure.

theProblem.title: A detector name is the wrong unit
lede: , five shapes. GitHub issues six. For a long time the sixth was simply not covered,

lede.b: and no rule list would have told you.

theProblem.claimSub: One file fixes that list, independently of what the code happens to catch.
theProblem.claim: The unit of a support claim is not “a detector we wrote” but “a credential a provider actually issues”.

theThreeInputs.title: Three files, three different questions
lede: They are kept apart on purpose:

lede.b: each one can be wrong on its own

facts.desc: A generator, from the core's detector registry.
One exact commit: the build the measurement ran against.
A flat list of detector ids and titles. Nothing about quality.
People, by hand, with a source link or a written note for every entry.
Nothing. It describes providers, not our code.

p.b: nobody can write one by hand.

p: The one-way direction matters: the matrix reads the taxonomy, and never the reverse. A rule in the code review makes it explicit —

p.b: variant support must not be inferred from a related family name.

p: Sharing a prefix with a supported token is not evidence.

whatARowSays.title: Provisional is arithmetic, not a feeling
lede: When a family falls short, the row carries
p: That family's token format is provider-documented, the best evidence tier there is. It was still only provisional, because the fixture coverage behind it was one positive case and three benign controls short.

p.b: Nobody can argue with that; somebody can go and write four fixtures.

p: Most of the matrix has since done exactly that.
